lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners can state the key differences between the religious and scientific views on the origins of man (Lesson 8).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recall the differences discussed in the previous lesson by asking two or three learners to state one difference each. 2. Ask: "Apart from their differences, can you think of anything that the religious view and the scientific view might agree on?" 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we look at what the religious and scientific views have in common."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Recall and state differences from the previous lesson. 2. Brainstorm possible similarities between the two views. 3. Listen attentively to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Explanation & Demonstration: Draw a Venn diagram on the chalkboard labelled "Religious View" and "Scientific View". 2. Similarity 1: Both views try to explain the same big question - how human beings came to exist. 3. Similarity 2: Both views agree that man began in a simpler/more basic form and became more complex or attained a special status over time (in religion, man is given dominion/is made vicegerent after creation; in science, simple life forms gradually became the complex modern human). 4. Similarity 3: Both views shape how people understand themselves, their place in the world, and how they should relate to other living things and to each other. 5. Similarity 4: Both views are respected and studied seriously by historians, and both continue to influence societies (including modern Zambian society) today. 6. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners discuss and list at least two additional similarities they can think of, and present them to the class for verification. 7. Real-Life Application: Explain that some Zambians, including scientists and religious leaders, hold both views together, believing, for example, that God may have used a process similar to evolution to bring about human life - showing that the two views are not always seen as mutually exclusive. 8. Synthesis: Summarise all similarities identified and emphasise that recognising common ground helps build tolerance and reduces unnecessary conflict between people of different beliefs.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Copy the Venn diagram of similarities (Fig 1.13). 2. Take notes on each of the similarities discussed. 3. Work in groups to identify and present additional similarities. 4. Relate the discussion to the real-life example of people who hold both views together. 5. Take notes on the synthesis and its citizenship message.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE similarity between the religious view and the scientific view on the origins of man. 2. Explain why recognising similarities between the religious and scientific views is important for national unity in Zambia. 3. Given the similarities and differences studied, explain to a younger learner at Mkushi Primary School, in TWO sentences, why it is possible for a person to respect both the religious and scientific views without necessarily choosing only one. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Guidance and Counselling Department at the school has noticed that some pupils have started mocking classmates who hold a different view (religious or scientific) on the origins of man, causing tension in class. You are asked, as a member of the History Club, to help resolve this. Task 1: State two similarities between the religious and scientific views on the origins of man. (6 marks) Task 2: Explain how these similarities can be used to reduce the tension among pupils. (7 marks) Task 3: Recommend one rule the class should adopt to ensure respectful discussion of this topic in future. (7 marks)
progression.learnersRole: 1. Read questions. 2. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Write a short paragraph titled 'What Religion and Science Agree On', using at least two similarities discussed in class, giving your own opinion on why this matters for unity in your school or community."
progression.learnersRole: Complete assignment.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Despite their differences, the religious and scientific views share important similarities: both try to explain how man came to exist, and both show man moving from a simpler state to a more complex or special one." 2. Preview: "Next, we will look at Zambian traditional/cultural views on the origins of man."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.3.1 Views on the Origins of Man
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Describing Zambian traditional/cultural beliefs on the origins of man, as a third view alongside religion and science.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to describe at least two Zambian traditional/cultural beliefs on the origins of man and explain their importance to national heritage.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.3); ECSEOL History Assessment Scheme (ECZ)
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Map of Zambia showing different ethnic groups (if available). Manila paper and markers. Copy of Fig 1.14 (illustrative map of Zambian traditional beliefs).
lesson_plans.rationale: Although the syllabus emphasises religious and scientific views, a comprehensive treatment of this topic in a Zambian classroom should also give learners a chance to explore their own cultural heritage, reinforcing the syllabus's stated aim of promoting Zambia's cultural roots (a key competence under Citizenship) and providing an additional real-life, Zambianised perspective before the final comparative lessons.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.3.1.1: Analyse religious and scientific views on the origins of man.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners can state similarities and differences between the religious and scientific views (Lessons 8-9).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Ask: "Before missionaries brought Christianity and Islam to Zambia, did our ancestors have their own beliefs about how human beings came to exist?" 2. Explain that many Zambian ethnic groups, such as the Bemba, Lozi and Tonga, had (and some still hold) their own traditional beliefs about a Creator and the beginning of mankind. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we describe Zambian traditional/cultural beliefs on the origins of man."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Share any traditional stories they may have heard from grandparents about a Creator or the beginning of people. 2. Listen to the explanation. 3. Listen attentively to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Explanation: Explain that most Zambian ethnic groups traditionally believed in a Supreme Being/Creator, even before the arrival of Christianity and Islam. Examples: the Bemba people traditionally referred to the Creator as Lesa; the Lozi people of Western Province believed in Nyambe as the Creator God who made mankind and taught early people important skills such as fire-making and farming; the Tonga people of Southern Province referred to the Supreme Being as Leza, closely linked to rain-making and the giving of life. 2. Draw/display the illustrative map (Fig 1.14) on the chalkboard, showing the common thread of belief in a Creator across different Zambian ethnic groups. 3. Group Activity: In groups of five (where possible, grouping learners of different home ethnic backgrounds together), learners share and record any traditional beliefs, proverbs, or stories about the origin of people known in their own family/home area, e.g. from Mkushi District's Lala/Swaka people or other areas represented in the class. 4. Real-Life Application: Relate this to National Heritage/Traditional Ceremonies (Topic 1.6), explaining that ceremonies such as the Kuomboka (Lozi), Ncwala (Ngoni), Likumbi Lya Mize (Luvale) or Umutomboko (Lunda) often include praise and reference to the Creator and the ancestors, keeping traditional beliefs about origins alive today. 5. Synthesis: Summarise that Zambian traditional beliefs form a third, valuable view on the origins of man that should be respected as part of the nation's cultural heritage, alongside the religious and scientific views.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Take notes on traditional Zambian beliefs about the Creator (e.g. Lesa, Nyambe, Leza). 2. Copy the illustrative map (Fig 1.14). 3. Work in groups to share and record beliefs/stories from their own home areas. 4. Relate traditional beliefs to a named Zambian traditional ceremony, e.g. Kuomboka, Ncwala or Umutomboko. 5. Take notes on the synthesis.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name the traditional term used by the Bemba people to refer to the Creator. 2. State ONE Zambian traditional belief about the origins of man, other than the Bemba example. 3. Mwaba, a Form 1 pupil at the school, says traditional beliefs about the Creator are "outdated" and have no connection to modern Zambian life. Explain to Mwaba ONE way traditional beliefs about the origins of man are still visible in Zambia today. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Ministry of Tourism is planning a Cultural Heritage Week in Mkushi District to promote Zambia's traditional beliefs and ceremonies to both local and international visitors. You are part of a team of Form 1 pupils from the school selected to research and present on traditional beliefs about the origins of man. Task 1: Name and describe two Zambian ethnic groups' traditional beliefs about the Creator. (8 marks) Task 2: Explain the importance of preserving such traditional beliefs for Zambia's national heritage. (6 marks) Task 3: Suggest one activity Cultural Heritage Week could include to showcase these beliefs to visitors. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: 1. Read questions. 2. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Ask an elder or grandparent in your home area what they know about your own ethnic group's traditional name for the Creator or their traditional belief about how the first people came to be. Write it down in a short paragraph."
progression.learnersRole: Complete assignment.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Many Zambian ethnic groups traditionally believed in a Supreme Being/Creator, such as Lesa (Bemba), Nyambe (Lozi) and Leza (Tonga), forming a valuable third view on the origins of man that is part of Zambia's cultural heritage." 2. Preview: "Next, we will hold a class debate comparing the religious and scientific views on the origins of man."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.3.1 Views on the Origins of Man
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Debating the religious and scientific views on the origins of man.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to construct and present at least two logical arguments for or against the motion "Science explains the origins of man better than religion", and practise respectful debating etiquette.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.3); ECSEOL History Assessment Scheme (ECZ)
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. A bell or whistle to signal speaking turns. Score sheet drawn on manila paper for the moderator. Motion written boldly on the chalkboard: 'Science explains the origins of man better than religion'. Copy of Fig 1.15 (debate structure diagram).
lesson_plans.rationale: Debating consolidates all the knowledge gained in Lessons 1-9 (religious accounts, scientific theory and evidence, similarities and differences) into a communication-based, competence-driven activity. It develops learners' critical thinking, public speaking confidence, and ability to defend a position using evidence, while reinforcing citizenship values such as respect for opposing views, mirroring the debate approach already used successfully in the school's Physical Education topic.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.3.1.1: Analyse religious and scientific views on the origins of man.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners can describe, compare and contrast the religious and scientific views on the origins of man (Lessons 1-9).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Write the motion on the chalkboard: "Science explains the origins of man better than religion." 2. Ask learners to raise hands: who agrees, who disagrees, who is undecided? 3. Explain debate rules briefly: each side gets equal speaking time, no shouting, respect the opponent's beliefs at all times. 4. State the lesson goal: "Today we debate on the religious and scientific views on the origins of man, using everything we have learnt this topic."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Read the motion on the board. 2. Raise hands to indicate their position. 3. Listen to and agree to follow the debate rules. 4. Listen attentively.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Explanation & Demonstration: Divide the class into a Proposing Team (Science explains it better) and an Opposing Team (Religion explains it better), with the rest as the Moderating Panel/Judges. 2. Give each team 8 minutes to prepare arguments using notes from Lessons 1-9 (Christian and Islamic accounts, Darwin's theory, fossil evidence, the timeline of life, similarities and differences). 3. Model one sample argument: "Science explains the origins of man better because its claims, such as the Broken Hill Skull found at Kabwe, can be tested and verified by other scientists, unlike religious claims which rely only on faith." 4. Conduct the debate: Proposing Team presents (3 minutes), Opposing Team presents (3 minutes), rebuttals (2 minutes each side), closing statements (1 minute each side). 5. Judging: The Moderating Panel scores each team on clarity, use of evidence, and respectfulness, using the score sheet. 6. Synthesis: Announce the outcome and summarise the strongest arguments from both sides on the chalkboard, emphasising that both religion and science offer valuable, complementary insights into a question that continues to be studied and discussed today.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Sit in assigned teams (Proposing, Opposing, Moderating Panel). 2. Prepare arguments in groups using earlier notes. 3. Listen to the sample argument as a model. 4. Present arguments, rebuttals and closing statements in an orderly manner. 5. Moderating Panel scores the teams using the score sheet. 6. Note the strongest arguments from both sides.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Write ONE argument in support of the motion 'Science explains the origins of man better than religion.' 2. Write ONE argument against the motion (i.e. in favour of religion). 3. After the debate, Simunji still insists that religion is "completely useless" because it cannot be proven in a laboratory. Using what was discussed in the debate, write a response correcting Simunji's view. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your school in Mkushi District has been invited to send a team to represent Central Province at a National Schools Debate Championship in Lusaka, with the motion 'Science explains the origins of man better than religion'. However, the same week has important end-of-term History continuous assessment for all Form 1 classes. The Head Teacher has asked the Debate Club to advise on how to balance both. Task 1: Argue for the importance of allowing pupils to attend the debate championship. (7 marks) Task 2: Argue for the importance of prioritising the History continuous assessment. (7 marks) Task 3: Propose one balanced solution that respects the importance of both activities. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: 1. Read questions. 2. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Write a half-page personal opinion essay titled 'What I Believe About the Origins of Man, and Why I Respect Other Views', using at least three points learnt in this topic."
progression.learnersRole: Complete assignment.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Both the religious and scientific views offer valuable, though different, explanations of the origins of man; a good historian studies both fairly and respects people who hold either view." 2. Preview: "Next, we will discuss how respecting different views on the origins of man promotes good citizenship in Zambia."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.3.1 Views on the Origins of Man
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Applying knowledge of the different views on the origins of man to promote tolerance, respect and good citizenship in Zambia.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to explain at least three ways in which respecting different views (religious, scientific and traditional) on the origins of man promotes tolerance and good citizenship in Zambia.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.3); ECSEOL History Assessment Scheme (ECZ)
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Manila paper and markers. Role-play cards describing short conflict scenarios. Copy of Fig 1.16 (citizenship wheel diagram).
lesson_plans.rationale: The specific competence for this topic requires learners not only to know the different views, but to analyse them. Analysis is incomplete without application: this lesson translates knowledge into a citizenship skill, addressing real tensions (religious intolerance, mockery of traditional beliefs, dismissiveness towards science) that can occur in Zambian schools and communities, directly building the Citizenship and Emotional Intelligence key competences of the syllabus.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.3.1.1: Analyse religious and scientific views on the origins of man.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners have studied the religious, scientific and traditional views on the origins of man and their similarities and differences, and have participated in a class debate (Lessons 1-11).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Ask: "Have you ever seen or heard of someone being mocked or excluded because of their religious belief, their acceptance of science, or their traditional/cultural beliefs, here in Mkushi District or elsewhere in Zambia?" 2. Allow two or three learners to briefly share (without naming individuals) any such experience they may have witnessed. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we discuss how respecting different views on the origins of man promotes tolerance and good citizenship."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Reflect on and share, respectfully and without naming individuals, any experience of intolerance witnessed. 2. Listen to classmates' experiences. 3. Listen attentively to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Explanation: Explain that Zambia is a multi-religious, multi-ethnic nation with the national motto "One Zambia, One Nation", and that respecting different views on sensitive topics such as the origins of man is an important part of good citizenship. 2. Present the citizenship wheel (Fig 1.16) showing four values: (i) Respect for religious beliefs; (ii) Respect for scientific knowledge; (iii) Respect for cultural/traditional views; (iv) Tolerance and unity in diversity. 3. Role-Play Activity: In groups of five, learners are given short role-play cards describing a conflict scenario (e.g. a Form 1 pupil mocking a classmate's church belief; a pupil dismissing traditional beliefs as "backward"; a pupil rejecting a scientific explanation without listening). Each group acts out the scenario and then a peaceful, respectful resolution. 4. Discussion: After each role-play, the class discusses what values (from the wheel) were shown or missing, and how the situation could be better handled. 5. Real-Life Application: Relate the discussion to national events such as Zambia's National Day of Prayer, Fasting, Repentance and Reconciliation, and to interfaith and inter-cultural cooperation seen in Zambian public life, showing that respecting diverse views is part of Zambia's national character. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the four citizenship values from the wheel and their importance for a peaceful, united Zambia.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Take notes on the meaning of citizenship in relation to this topic. 2. Copy the citizenship wheel diagram (Fig 1.16). 3. Participate in group role-plays, acting out both a conflict and its peaceful resolution. 4. Discuss which citizenship values were shown or missing in each role-play. 5. Relate the discussion to a real national example, e.g. the National Day of Prayer. 6. Take notes on the synthesis.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE citizenship value that helps learners respect people who hold a different view on the origins of man. 2. Explain why Zambia's national motto 'One Zambia, One Nation' is relevant to this topic. 3. During a class discussion, Nawa openly laughs at a classmate, Fweta, for believing the traditional Tonga account of creation instead of the scientific one. Explain to Nawa TWO reasons why this behaviour is wrong, and suggest what Nawa should do instead. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Guidance and Counselling Department, working with the History Department at the school, has been asked by the Provincial Education Office to design a short 'Unity in Diversity' campaign for Form 1 pupils across Central Province, using the topic of the origins of man as a starting point. Task 1: Explain how knowledge of the religious, scientific and traditional views on the origins of man can help promote unity among pupils of different backgrounds. (8 marks) Task 2: Suggest two activities the campaign could include to teach tolerance using this topic. (6 marks) Task 3: Explain one way such a campaign could benefit Zambia as a nation in the long run. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: 1. Read questions. 2. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Design a simple poster (on a sheet of paper) with the slogan 'Different Views, One Zambia', illustrating at least two of the views on the origins of man (religious, scientific, traditional) living together in unity."
progression.learnersRole: Complete assignment.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Respecting different views on the origins of man - religious, scientific and traditional - builds tolerance, reduces conflict, and strengthens the unity called for by Zambia's motto, 'One Zambia, One Nation'." 2. Preview: "Next, we will revise the whole topic and practise ECSEOL-style examination questions on the origins of man."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.3.1 Views on the Origins of Man
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Revision and consolidation of Topic 1.3 (The Origins of Man), with practice of ECSEOL-style examination questions.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to correctly answer a range of revision questions, including ECSEOL-style scenario questions, covering the religious, scientific and traditional views on the origins of man and their similarities and differences.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.3); ECSEOL History Assessment Scheme (ECZ)
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Revision mind-map on manila paper. Printed/copied revision question cards for group work. Copy of Fig 1.17 (revision mind-map).
lesson_plans.rationale: This final lesson in the topic consolidates all ten preceding lessons into an examination-focused revision session, giving learners guided practice in the exact scenario-based question style used in the ECSEOL Final Examination (Component 2) and School-Based Assessment (Component 1), as described in the ECZ History Assessment Scheme, thereby preparing them for both continuous assessment and the final examination.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.3.1.1: Analyse religious and scientific views on the origins of man.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners have covered all aspects of Topic 1.3: religious views (Christianity and Islam), scientific views (Darwin's theory, fossil evidence, the timeline of life), Zambian traditional views, similarities, differences, and citizenship applications (Lessons 1-12).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Ask learners to close their books and, as a whole class, quickly call out anything they remember from the topic so far (a "popcorn" recall activity). 2. List learners' responses briefly on the chalkboard without correcting yet. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we revise the whole topic on the Origins of Man and practise ECSEOL-style examination questions."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Call out facts remembered from the topic (e.g. "Charles Darwin", "Adam and Eve", "Broken Hill Skull", "Lesa"). 2. Observe the list building on the chalkboard. 3. Listen attentively to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Explanation & Demonstration: Display the completed revision mind-map (Fig 1.17), showing the four branches: Religious View, Scientific View, Zambian Traditional View, and Contrasts/Similarities, correcting and organising the learners' earlier "popcorn" list under the correct branch. 2. Explain the ECSEOL question style clearly: examination and continuous assessment questions are usually presented as a real-life scenario, followed by tasks (a), (b), (c) or Task 1, 2, 3, each carrying specific marks, and learners must apply their knowledge to the scenario rather than simply recalling facts. 3. Guided Practice: Work through one full ECSEOL-style scenario question as a class (see Exercise Question 4 below), modelling how to identify what each task is asking and how to structure a full-mark answer. 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners are given different revision question cards (one card per group, covering a different sub-topic: Christianity, Islam, Darwin's theory, fossil evidence/timeline, Zambian traditional views, or similarities/differences) to answer together and then present their answers to the class for checking. 5. Peer Marking: Groups exchange answers and mark each other's work using model answers provided by the teacher, building assessment literacy. 6. Synthesis: Recap the whole topic using the mind-map, and remind learners of the importance of reading each scenario carefully before answering in the examination.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Watch as the teacher organises the class's earlier recall list into the mind-map. 2. Copy the completed revision mind-map (Fig 1.17). 3. Take notes on how to approach ECSEOL-style scenario questions. 4. Follow the guided practice question as a class. 5. Work in groups on assigned revision question cards and present answers to the class. 6. Exchange and mark another group's answers using the model answers provided.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State the FOUR main branches of this topic as shown on the revision mind-map. 2. In the ECSEOL examination format, how are History questions usually presented, and how many tasks/marks does each scenario typically carry? 3. Explain briefly why it is important, before answering an ECSEOL-style scenario question, to read the scenario carefully and identify exactly what each task requires. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION (FULL PRACTICE ITEM - EoC1: Demonstrates understanding of the ideologies of Evolution and early civilisation): You are the Chairperson of the History Club at the school. The Provincial Education Office in Central Province has selected your club to host a Provincial Quiz Competition on 'The Origins of Man', where teams from schools such as Serenje Girls Technical School, Kabwe Secondary School and Ndola Girls Technical School will compete. As Chairperson, you are asked to prepare the official model answers for the quiz masters. Task 1: Describe how man was created according to EITHER the Christian OR the Islamic account. (7 marks) Task 2: Explain how Charles Darwin's Theory of Evolution suggests man came to exist. (7 marks) Task 3: Suggest two ways the quiz competition can help promote unity and tolerance among the participating schools from different parts of Zambia. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: 1. Read questions. 2. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Using your notes from all lessons on the Origins of Man, write your own ECSEOL-style scenario question (with a short real-life scenario and two tasks with marks) on any part of this topic, together with your own model answers. Be ready to exchange your question with a classmate next lesson."
progression.learnersRole: Complete assignment.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "We have now covered the full topic of the Origins of Man: the Christian and Islamic religious accounts, the scientific view through Darwin's theory and fossil evidence, Zambian traditional beliefs, and how all these views compare and can be respected together as good citizens." 2. Preview: "Next, we move to a new topic: The Stone Age, where we will study the earliest known human societies and their way of life."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.1 The Way of Life in Stone Age
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Classifying the Stone Age into its three periods: Early Stone Age (Palaeolithic), Middle Stone Age (Mesolithic) and Late Stone Age (Neolithic).
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to classify the Stone Age into three periods and state the alternative name and approximate duration of each period.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.1: The Way of Life in Stone Age).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed/drawn timeline chart of the three Stone Age periods. A plain stone or pebble (as a prop). Manila paper and markers for group work.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson lays the foundation for the whole topic. Before learners study who lived during the Stone Age or how they lived, they must first understand that the Stone Age itself is divided into three distinct periods based on how advanced the stone tools were. Using Zambian archaeological examples (Kabwe, Mumbwa) grounds an abstract idea in familiar geography, building analytical thinking and communication competences from the outset.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Classifying the Stone Age).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners already know the meaning of History and have learnt about the Origins of Man (religious and scientific views) from Topic 1.3.

progression.teacherRole: Show learners a plain stone and ask, "What do you think our ancestors used a stone like this for, long before metal tools were discovered?" Explain that today's lesson goes back to the very beginning of human history, before iron working, to a time called the Stone Age. State the lesson goal: "Today we classify the Stone Age into its three periods."
progression.learnersRole: Suggest possible uses of the stone, e.g. cutting, hunting, digging. Listen attentively as the teacher introduces the Stone Age. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: Define the Stone Age: the earliest and longest period of human history when people made and used tools mainly from stone, before the discovery of metal. Explain that historians classify the Stone Age into three periods based on how advanced the stone tools were: Early Stone Age (Palaeolithic/Old Stone Age), Middle Stone Age (Mesolithic) and Late Stone Age (Neolithic/New Stone Age). Display the timeline (Fig 1.4a) and explain the approximate duration of each period. Zambian example: Early and Middle Stone Age tools have been found at Kabwe (Broken Hill) and Mumbwa Caves in Central Province, while Late Stone Age tools and rock art have been found at Nachikufu Caves near Mpika in Muchinga Province. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners draw their own timeline on manila paper, labelling the three periods and one Zambian site under each. Synthesis: Summarise the three periods and their alternative names on the chalkboard.
progression.learnersRole: Copy the meaning of the Stone Age. Note the three periods of the Stone Age and their alternative names. Copy the timeline into their notebooks. Note the Zambian examples given. Work in groups to draw and label a timeline with a Zambian site under each period. Copy the summarised classification from the chalkboard.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define the term Stone Age. 2. Name the three periods of the Stone Age. 3. Chomba, a Form 1 pupil at Kabulonga Girls Secondary School in Lusaka, argues that the Stone Age was "just one long period with no changes." Using what you have learnt, explain to Chomba TWO reasons why this statement is not correct. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the History Club at your school. The club has been invited to mount a small display for Heritage Week showing how early Zambians lived before farming and iron working began. Task 1: Explain to visitors what the Stone Age is. (4 marks) Task 2: Name and briefly describe the three periods of the Stone Age that your display should represent. (10 marks) Task 3: Suggest one Zambian site your club could use as an example for each period. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Using a ruler, draw a timeline in your exercise book showing the three periods of the Stone Age in the correct order, and next to each period write one Zambian place where tools from that period have been found."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment and plan the timeline.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "The Stone Age is classified into the Early, Middle and Late Stone Age, based on how advanced the tools were." Preview: "Next, we will identify the actual human ancestor who lived during the Early Stone Age."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.1 The Way of Life in Stone Age
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Identifying the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age — Homo Habilis.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to describe Homo Habilis and explain why this human ancestor is important to the study of the Early Stone Age in Africa and Zambia.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.1: The Way of Life in Stone Age).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed or drawn picture of Homo Habilis. A few rounded pebbles to represent simple 'Oldowan' pebble tools. Manila paper for group work.
lesson_plans.rationale: Having classified the Stone Age into three periods in Lesson 1, learners now examine the actual human ancestor who lived in the Early Stone Age. This lesson links directly to the scientific view of the origins of man learnt in Topic 1.3, deepening learners' critical thinking as they analyse physical and behavioural evidence.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Identifying the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners can classify the Stone Age into three periods (from Lesson 1) and know the scientific (Charles Darwin) view on the origins of man from Topic 1.3.

progression.teacherRole: Ask learners to recall the three periods of the Stone Age learnt in the previous lesson. Show a drawing of an early human-like skull and ask, "Who do you think this creature is, and in which Stone Age period did it live?" State the lesson goal: "Today we identify and describe the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age."
progression.learnersRole: Recall and state the three periods of the Stone Age. Observe the picture and give suggestions. Listen attentively.

progression.teacherRole: Explain that the human ancestor commonly studied for the Early Stone Age is Homo Habilis ("Handy Man"), believed to be among the earliest tool-making ancestors, living roughly 2.6 million to 1.5 million years ago mainly in East and Southern Africa. Describe features: smaller brain than modern humans; walked upright on two legs; made simple, rough pebble tools (Oldowan tools) for cutting and pounding; lived in small family groups; gathered wild plants and scavenged meat. Zambian/regional link: Early Stone Age tool evidence associated with such early toolmakers has been found in the Broken Hill (Kabwe) area and other Central African sites, showing early humans occupied this region. Group Activity: In pairs, learners list THREE features that made Homo Habilis different from modern humans and ONE way Homo Habilis was similar to modern humans. Role Play: Two learners mime how an Early Stone Age person might use a pebble tool to cut meat or crack a bone, while classmates guess the activity. Synthesis: Summarise features of Homo Habilis on the board under two headings: 'Similar to us' and 'Different from us'.
progression.learnersRole: Copy the description of Homo Habilis. Note the features of Homo Habilis under similarities and differences. Note the Zambian/regional link given. Work in pairs to list differences and one similarity with modern humans. Two learners perform the role play; the rest guess the activity. Copy the summarised features from the chalkboard.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name the human ancestor associated with the Early Stone Age. 2. State TWO features of Homo Habilis. 3. Musonda tells his young brother that "the first humans looked and lived exactly like people today." Using what you have learnt about Homo Habilis, explain TWO reasons why Musonda is wrong. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a tour guide trainee at a museum in Livingstone that has a display on human origins. A group of visiting Form 1 pupils from Munali Secondary School in Lusaka asks you to explain the earliest tool-making humans. Task 1: Identify the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age and explain what the name means. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE features of this ancestor's way of life. (10 marks) Task 3: Explain why studying such ancestors is important for understanding Zambia's history. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Draw and label a simple picture of Homo Habilis using a stone tool, showing at least two features that make it different from a modern human."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment and plan the drawing.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "Homo Habilis, the 'Handy Man', was the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age, known for simple pebble tools." Preview: "Next, we will identify the human ancestors of the Middle and Late Stone Age."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.1 The Way of Life in Stone Age
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Identifying the human ancestors of the Middle Stone Age (Broken Hill Man) and the Late Stone Age (Bushmen/San).
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to describe Broken Hill Man and the Bushmen/San, and explain where evidence of their existence has been found in Zambia.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.1: The Way of Life in Stone Age).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed or drawn picture of the Broken Hill (Kabwe) Skull. A map of Zambia showing Kabwe and Kasama. Manila paper for group work.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson builds on Lesson 2 by completing the sequence of human ancestors across the three Stone Age periods. Because the skull of Broken Hill Man was discovered in Kabwe, Zambia, this lesson strongly builds citizenship and national pride while developing analytical thinking.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Identifying the human ancestors of the Middle and Late Stone Age).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners can describe Homo Habilis as the Early Stone Age human ancestor (from Lesson 2).

progression.teacherRole: Ask learners to recall Homo Habilis and the Stone Age period he belonged to. Narrate: "In 1921, miners at Broken Hill Mine in Kabwe, Zambia, discovered an old human skull while digging for lead and zinc. This skull became famous the world over." Ask: "Which Stone Age period do you think this skull might belong to?" State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: Recall and state facts about Homo Habilis. Listen to the story and give suggestions. Listen attentively.

progression.teacherRole: Explain that the Middle Stone Age human ancestor commonly studied is Broken Hill Man (also called Rhodesian Man / Homo rhodesiensis / Kabwe Man), whose skull was discovered at Kabwe, Zambia in 1921. Broken Hill Man had a larger brain than Homo Habilis and made improved, sharper stone tools. Explain that the Late Stone Age human ancestor commonly studied is the Bushmen (San people) - small hunter-gatherer communities known for fine, small stone tools (microliths), bows and arrows, and rock art, some of which can still be seen in Zambia at Mwela Rocks near Kasama and Nsalu Cave. Compare the two on the chalkboard: Middle Stone Age (Broken Hill Man) - improved tools, larger brain, found at Kabwe; Late Stone Age (Bushmen/San) - finest tools, rock art, found at Mwela Rocks and Nachikufu. Group Activity: Divide the class into two groups. Group A researches and lists facts about Broken Hill Man; Group B lists facts about the Bushmen/San, using notes and manila paper. Gallery Walk: Groups display and present their findings to the class. Synthesis: Complete a three-ancestor summary on the chalkboard: Homo Habilis (Early) - Broken Hill Man (Middle) - Bushmen/San (Late).
progression.learnersRole: Take notes on Broken Hill Man and his discovery at Kabwe. Take notes on the Bushmen/San and their rock art. Copy the comparison from the chalkboard. Work in assigned groups to research and record facts. Present group findings during the gallery walk. Copy the completed three-ancestor summary.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Where in Zambia was the skull of Broken Hill Man discovered, and in which year? 2. Name the Late Stone Age human ancestor known for fine tools and rock art. 3. A tourist visiting Kabwe asks Nchimunya, a Form 1 pupil, why the town is important in the history of human origins. Using what you have learnt, help Nchimunya give TWO correct reasons. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a tour guide at a cultural centre near Kasama that displays rock art believed to have been made by the San people. A group of visiting researchers wants to understand the human story behind the site. Task 1: Identify the human ancestor group associated with the Late Stone Age rock art. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE features of the way of life of this Late Stone Age ancestor. (10 marks) Task 3: Explain the importance of the Broken Hill Man discovery in Kabwe to Zambia's history. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Interview an elderly family member or neighbour about any old rock paintings, caves or 'ancient stones' they know of in your area, and write three sentences about what they told you."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment and plan whom to interview.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "The three human ancestors of the Stone Age are Homo Habilis (Early), Broken Hill Man (Middle) and the Bushmen/San (Late)." Preview: "Next, we will discuss the social aspects of life in the Stone Age."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.1 The Way of Life in Stone Age
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Describing the social aspects of Stone Age life: family/band life, division of labour, communication and beliefs.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to explain at least three social aspects of Stone Age life.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.1: The Way of Life in Stone Age).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Manila paper divided into columns. Picture/description of a family band (drawn).
lesson_plans.rationale: Having identified the human ancestors in Lessons 2 and 3, learners now examine how Stone Age people organised themselves socially. Splitting 'social, political and economic aspects' into three focused lessons allows adequate depth and hands-on activity time for each, in line with competence-based teaching principles.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Describing social aspects of the Stone Age).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners can describe the human ancestors of the three Stone Age periods (from Lessons 2 and 3).

progression.teacherRole: Ask: "If you had no phone, no school and no shops, how would you and your family survive together?" Explain that Stone Age people lived in small family groups called bands, and today's lesson explores their social life. State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: Suggest ways a family could survive together without modern conveniences. Listen attentively. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: Explain social organisation: Stone Age people lived in small bands/family groups of about 20-30 people, related by blood or marriage, who moved together in search of food. Explain cooperation and division of labour: men mostly hunted; women and children gathered wild fruits, roots and insects; all members cared for the young and the old; children learnt skills directly from parents and elders since there were no formal schools. Explain communication and beliefs: Stone Age people communicated using simple language and gestures, and expressed daily life and beliefs through rock art/paintings, e.g. at Mwela Rocks (Kasama) and Nsalu Cave. Real-life link: Compare to a modern Zambian extended family working together on a farm in, for example, Chibombo District, where every member has a role - showing that cooperation as a value has continued into today's society. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners role-play a 'Stone Age band' preparing for a day, assigning roles (hunters, gatherers, child-minders, tool-makers) and acting out a short cooperative scene on the school playground. Synthesis: List social features on the chalkboard under 'Family/band life', 'Division of labour' and 'Communication and beliefs'.
progression.learnersRole: Take notes on band/family life. Take notes on division of labour between men, women and children. Take notes on communication and beliefs, including rock art. Give own examples of modern family cooperation, e.g. from their home area. Work in groups to role-play a Stone Age band's daily activities. Copy the summarised social features from the chalkboard.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. What is a 'band' in relation to Stone Age social life? 2. State TWO ways men and women shared work in a Stone Age band. 3. Chalwe says people in the Stone Age "lived alone and cared only for themselves." Using what you have learnt about social life, explain to Chalwe why this is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your school's Cultural and Heritage Club has been asked to perform a short skit for Independence Day, showing how early Zambians lived together as families before modern institutions like schools and hospitals existed. Task 1: Explain what a Stone Age 'band' was. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE social practices your skit should show, such as division of labour and care for the young and old. (10 marks) Task 3: Suggest one way the skit could link Stone Age cooperation to values Zambians still practise today, such as community spirit. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Write a paragraph describing how your own family or neighbours in your community cooperate and share duties today, and compare this to Stone Age band life."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment and plan the paragraph.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "Stone Age people lived in family bands, shared work between men, women and children, and communicated through simple language and rock art." Preview: "Next, we will discuss the political aspects of life in the Stone Age."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.1 The Way of Life in Stone Age
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Describing the political aspects of Stone Age life: leadership, decision-making and conflict resolution.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to explain how Stone Age bands were led and how decisions and conflicts were handled.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.1: The Way of Life in Stone Age).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Manila paper for group work. Picture/description of a band elder or headman (drawn).
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson continues the three-part breakdown of social, political and economic aspects begun in Lesson 4. Focusing specifically on political life builds citizenship competence, as learners compare early informal leadership with the formal leadership structures they know today.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Describing political aspects of the Stone Age).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the social organisation of Stone Age bands (from Lesson 4).

progression.teacherRole: Ask: "Who makes the big decisions in your home or community today, for example a Chief, a Headman or your parents?" Explain that even without governments, courts or police, Stone Age bands still had ways of leading themselves and settling disputes. State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: Give examples of leaders/decision-makers they know in their homes or communities. Listen attentively. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: Explain leadership: Stone Age bands were led informally by the oldest or most experienced/skilled member (e.g. the best hunter or an elder), not by kings, chiefs or a formal government; leadership was based on ability and respect, not inheritance. Explain decision-making: important decisions, such as when to move camp or where to hunt, were made through discussion among the adult members of the band, similar to a small community meeting. Explain conflict resolution: disputes were settled informally through discussion or mediation by elders; in serious cases the band could split into smaller groups; there were no formal written laws, courts or police. Zambian real-life link: compare to how a village today, for example in Mkushi or Chinsali, may still settle small disputes through a Village Headman or Induna before involving formal police or courts, showing that informal leadership has continued in modified form. Group Activity/Role Play: In groups, learners role-play a 'band meeting' deciding where to move camp because water has dried up, showing discussion and consensus-building. Synthesis: Chalkboard summary - 'Leadership: skill/age-based; Decision-making: group discussion; Justice: informal, elder-mediated'.
progression.learnersRole: Take notes on how leaders were chosen in Stone Age bands. Take notes on how decisions were made. Take notes on how disputes were resolved. Give own examples of informal leadership in their community. Work in groups to role-play a band meeting and decision-making process. Copy the summarised political features from the chalkboard.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. How were leaders chosen in a Stone Age band? 2. State ONE way disputes were settled in Stone Age bands. 3. Mumba argues that the Stone Age had "no leadership at all." Using what you have learnt, correct Mumba's statement with TWO points. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Civic Education and History Clubs at Ndeke Secondary School in Kabwe have been asked to compare early forms of leadership with leadership in Zambia today, for a Democracy Week debate. Task 1: Explain how leadership operated in a Stone Age band. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE features of political/leadership life in the Stone Age, such as decision-making and dispute settlement. (10 marks) Task 3: Suggest one way modern Zambian society has improved on Stone Age methods of leadership and justice. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Ask a parent or guardian how disagreements are settled in your home area, for example by a headman, church elder or community leader, and write two sentences comparing this to Stone Age conflict resolution."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment and plan whom to ask.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "Stone Age bands were led informally by the most skilled or respected members, and decisions and disputes were handled through discussion rather than formal government." Preview: "Next, we will discuss the economic aspects of life in the Stone Age."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.1 The Way of Life in Stone Age
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Describing the economic aspects of Stone Age life: hunting, gathering, fishing and simple exchange.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to explain how Stone Age people obtained and shared food and resources.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.1: The Way of Life in Stone Age).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. A few natural objects (leaves, seeds, small stones) for a foraging simulation. Manila paper for group work.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson completes the three-part breakdown of social, political and economic aspects. It links to Financial Literacy by introducing learners to the earliest, simplest forms of economic activity and exchange, long before money existed.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Describing economic aspects of the Stone Age).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the social and political aspects of Stone Age life (from Lessons 4 and 5).

progression.teacherRole: Take learners to the school playground (or use the classroom) and ask them to find and collect three natural objects (leaves, seeds, small stones) within two minutes, as Stone Age gatherers would have done. Ask: "How did it feel searching for food or resources without a shop nearby?" State the lesson goal: "Today we discuss how the Stone Age economy worked."
progression.learnersRole: Search for and collect three natural objects within the given time. Respond about how the search felt. Listen attentively.

progression.teacherRole: Explain that the Stone Age economy was a subsistence economy, based on hunting, gathering and, in some areas, fishing - there was no farming, money or formal trade as known today. Explain hunting: men used spears, and later bows and arrows, to kill wild animals such as antelope for meat, skins and bones. Explain gathering: women and children collected wild fruits, roots, tubers, honey and insects, forming the largest part of the diet. Explain fishing: bands living near rivers and lakes such as the Kafue and Zambezi supplemented their diet with fish, caught using simple traps, spears or nets made from plant fibres. Explain sharing/exchange: food obtained was shared among all members of the band; some bands exchanged surplus items, such as skins and shells, with neighbouring bands - an early, simple form of exchange without money. Group Activity: In groups, learners create a 'menu for one day in the life of a Stone Age family' using Zambian wildlife/plant examples, e.g. impala meat, wild loquats (masuku), honey and Kafue bream, and complete the Fig 1.4c wheel diagram combining social, political and economic aspects.
progression.learnersRole: Take notes on the meaning of a subsistence economy. Take notes on hunting as an economic activity. Take notes on gathering as an economic activity. Take notes on fishing and sharing/exchange. Work in groups to design a Stone Age 'daily menu' using Zambian examples. Copy the completed three-aspect wheel diagram (social, political, economic).

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name the THREE main economic activities of Stone Age people. 2. What is meant by a 'subsistence economy'? 3. Bupe insists that Stone Age people "had no way of getting food without shops." Using what you have learnt, correct Bupe with TWO points. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Young Historians Club at a school near the Kafue River. The club wants to create an exhibition comparing how early Zambians near rivers survived economically with how communities along the Kafue River earn a living today. Task 1: Explain the term 'subsistence economy' as used in the Stone Age. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE ways Stone Age people obtained food and resources. (10 marks) Task 3: Compare one Stone Age economic activity with a similar modern economic activity practised along the Kafue River today, such as fishing. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Write a short paragraph listing THREE wild foods (fruits, plants, animals or fish) found in your area that Stone Age people might have relied on, and explain how people in your community use similar resources today."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment and plan the paragraph.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "Stone Age people survived through a subsistence economy based on hunting, gathering, fishing and simple sharing/exchange." Preview: "Next, we will analyse the tools that Stone Age people used for hunting, cutting and digging."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.1 The Way of Life in Stone Age
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Analysing the use of various Stone Age tools: hunting, cutting and digging tools.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to identify Stone Age tools and explain their uses in hunting, cutting and digging.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.1: The Way of Life in Stone Age).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. A few real stones/pebbles for demonstration. Printed pictures of hand axes, spearheads and scrapers. Manila paper for group work.
lesson_plans.rationale: Having covered social, political and economic aspects, learners now examine the technology (tools) that underpinned that way of life. This develops analytical thinking and helps learners appreciate that early Zambian communities already possessed real, purposeful technology.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Analysing the use of various Stone Age tools).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the economic activities of the Stone Age (from Lesson 6).

progression.teacherRole: Pass around a smooth stone and a sharp-edged stone and ask learners which one would be more useful for cutting meat, and why. Explain that today's lesson looks at the actual tools Stone Age people made and used. State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: Examine the two stones and give reasoned answers. Listen attentively. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: Explain that Stone Age people shaped stones, mainly by chipping/flaking, into tools for specific tasks; tools became sharper and more specialised from the Early to the Late Stone Age. Explain hunting tools: spears and, later, bows with arrow heads, used to kill animals such as buffalo and antelope. Explain cutting tools: hand axes and stone knives/flakes, used to cut meat, skin animals and cut plant material. Explain digging tools: digging sticks, sometimes stone-tipped, and scrapers, used to dig up roots and tubers and to prepare hides. Zambian link: such tools have been excavated at Mumbwa Caves, Kalambo Falls and Kabwe, showing Zambia has rich Stone Age tool evidence used by archaeologists to study our past. Group Activity: In groups, learners match pictures/descriptions of tools to their correct use (hunting/cutting/digging) on a worksheet drawn on manila paper, and present their answers.
progression.learnersRole: Take notes on hunting tools with examples. Take notes on cutting tools with examples. Take notes on digging tools with examples. Note the Zambian archaeological link. Work in groups to match tools to their correct use. Present group answers to the class.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name TWO tools Stone Age people used for hunting. 2. What was a digging stick used for? 3. Kabaso says "a hand axe and a spear were used for exactly the same purpose." Using what you have learnt, explain to Kabaso why this is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The National Museums Board has asked your school's History Club to help set up labels for a Stone Age tools exhibition at the Livingstone Museum. Task 1: Identify the THREE main uses of Stone Age tools covered in this lesson. (6 marks) Task 2: For each use (hunting, cutting, digging), name and describe a suitable Stone Age tool. (9 marks) Task 3: Explain why studying such tools helps historians understand how Stone Age people lived. (5 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Draw and label three Stone Age tools (one for hunting, one for cutting and one for digging), and write one sentence explaining the use of each."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment and plan the drawings.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "Stone Age tools were used mainly for hunting, cutting and digging, and became more advanced over time." Preview: "Next, we will contrast the Stone Age way of life with modern way of life."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.1 The Way of Life in Stone Age
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Contrasting the Stone Age way of life with the modern way of life.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to compare and contrast the Stone Age way of life with modern way of life using at least three similarities and three differences.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.1: The Way of Life in Stone Age).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Large Venn diagram drawn on manila paper (two overlapping circles). Colour markers or crayons. Exercise books.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson consolidates Lessons 1 to 7 into a comparative, critical-thinking activity, helping learners appreciate continuity and change over time - a core historical skill - while linking the ancient past meaningfully to their own modern lives in Zambia.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Contrasting Stone Age way of life with modern way of life).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners have covered the classification, ancestors, social, political and economic aspects, and tools of the Stone Age (from Lessons 1 to 7).

progression.teacherRole: Ask learners to imagine spending one full day living exactly like a Stone Age person, with no phone, no shop and no built house. Ask: "What would be the hardest part?" Explain that today's lesson compares Stone Age life with life today. State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: Respond with what they think would be hardest, e.g. finding food, staying safe. Listen attentively. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: Draw a large Venn diagram on the chalkboard labelled 'Stone Age Life' and 'Modern Life'. Similarities: guide learners to identify common features - both need food, shelter and clothing; both use tools; both live in groups/communities; both have some form of leadership. Differences - Stone Age: lived in caves/rock shelters, nomadic (moved often), used stone tools, obtained food by hunting/gathering, no formal schools or hospitals, no money. Differences - Modern: live in built houses, for example in Lusaka, Kitwe or rural villages with brick homes; settled/permanent; use metal/machine tools and technology; obtain food through farming/formal jobs and buying from markets/shops; have schools, hospitals and money/banks. Group Activity: In pairs, learners sort five given statements into the correct part of the Venn diagram, e.g. 'used stone tools', 'lives in a brick house in Kitwe', 'gathers wild fruits for food', 'goes to Levy Mwanawasa Hospital when sick', 'needs food and shelter'. Synthesis: Review answers as a class and correct any misclassifications.
progression.learnersRole: Copy the Venn diagram frame into their books. Contribute similarities to be written in the overlapping section. Note differences under Stone Age Life. Note differences under Modern Life. Work in pairs to classify the five statements correctly. Correct their diagrams based on class feedback.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State TWO similarities between Stone Age life and modern life. 2. State TWO differences between Stone Age life and modern life. 3. Kondwani says "modern people no longer need tools like Stone Age people did." Using what you have learnt, explain why Kondwani's statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your school in Chipata has organised a 'Then and Now' exhibition for Founder's Day, comparing Stone Age life with life in modern Zambia. Task 1: State TWO ways Stone Age people obtained shelter and food, and compare each with how people in Chipata obtain shelter and food today. (8 marks) Task 2: Explain TWO differences in technology/tools between the Stone Age and modern Zambia. (8 marks) Task 3: Suggest one lesson modern Zambians can learn from the way Stone Age people cooperated as a community. (4 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Draw your own Venn diagram at home comparing how your grandparents grew up and how you live today, with at least two similarities and two differences."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "Stone Age life and modern life share basic human needs, but differ greatly in tools, shelter, food sources and technology." Preview: "Next, we will locate Stone Age sites on the map of Zambia."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.2 Stone Age Sites in Zambia
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Locating Stone Age sites on the map of Zambia, e.g. Mumbwa Caves, Nachikufu Caves, Gwisho Hot Springs.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to locate and name at least four Stone Age sites on a map of Zambia.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.2: Stone Age Sites in Zambia).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed or drawn outline map of Zambia. Coloured dots/stickers or markers. Atlases (if available).
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson moves the topic from the Stone Age way of life (1.4.1) to Zambia's physical Stone Age heritage sites (1.4.2). Mapping skills build analytical and digital literacy competences, and prepare learners for the next lesson on the tourism and cultural value of these sites.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.2.1: Assess importance of Stone Age sites in Zambia (Locating Stone Age sites on the map of Zambia).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the way of life, ancestors and tools of the Stone Age (from Lessons 1 to 8).

progression.teacherRole: Display or draw a blank outline map of Zambia and ask learners to name any historical or heritage site they already know, for example Victoria Falls. Explain that many places in Zambia hold evidence of Stone Age life, and today we will locate some of them. State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: Name heritage sites they already know. Listen attentively. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: Explain that archaeologists have discovered Stone Age tools, bones and rock art at several sites across Zambia, mainly in caves, rock shelters and near water sources. Introduce and locate key sites on the map: Mumbwa Caves (Central Province) - Early/Middle Stone Age tools; Nachikufu Caves (Mpika, Muchinga Province) - Late Stone Age tools and rock paintings; Gwisho Hot Springs (Kafue Flats, Southern Province) - Late Stone Age site with well-preserved remains near hot springs; Kalambo Falls (Mbala, Northern Province) - one of the oldest and most important Early Stone Age sites in Africa; Mwela Rocks (near Kasama, Northern Province) - rock art site. For each site, briefly state what was found there and why it matters. Group Activity: In groups, learners use an outline map of Zambia drawn on manila paper to mark and label at least four Stone Age sites, referring to an atlas or wall map for correct province locations. Presentations: Groups present their labelled maps to the class. Synthesis: Complete a class map on the chalkboard showing all sites discussed.
progression.learnersRole: Take notes on Mumbwa Caves and their location. Take notes on Nachikufu Caves and their location. Take notes on Gwisho Hot Springs, Kalambo Falls and Mwela Rocks. Note what was found at each site. Work in groups to mark and label at least four sites on an outline map. Present group maps to the class.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name TWO Stone Age sites found in Zambia. 2. In which province is Kalambo Falls located? 3. Temba, a Form 1 pupil from Solwezi, believes Stone Age sites are "only found outside Zambia." Using what you have learnt, correct Temba with TWO examples. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Ministry of Tourism has invited your school's Geography-History Club to help produce a simple tourist map brochure showing Stone Age heritage sites in Zambia for visitors attending a conference in Lusaka. Task 1: Name and locate (by province) FOUR Stone Age sites in Zambia that should appear on the brochure map. (12 marks) Task 2: For any ONE of the sites named, briefly state what was discovered there. (4 marks) Task 3: Suggest one reason why accurately locating such sites on a map is useful for visitors and researchers. (4 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Using an atlas or map of Zambia, draw the outline of your own Province and mark any historical, cultural or Stone Age site you know of in it, or the nearest one to you."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment and identify their Province.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "Zambia has several important Stone Age sites, including Mumbwa Caves, Nachikufu Caves, Gwisho Hot Springs, Kalambo Falls and Mwela Rocks." Preview: "Next, we will assess the importance of these Stone Age sites, focusing on tourism and cultural heritage."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.4.2 Stone Age Sites in Zambia
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Analysing the importance of Stone Age sites in Zambia, focusing on tourism and cultural heritage, and how to conserve them.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to explain at least three reasons why Stone Age sites are important to Zambia and suggest ways to conserve them.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4.2: Stone Age Sites in Zambia).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Picture/story of a Zambian heritage site attracting tourists. Manila paper for poster-making.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson completes Topic 1.4 by moving from identifying and locating sites (Lesson 9) to evaluating their value. It connects to Entrepreneurship and Financial Literacy through business opportunities at heritage sites, and to Environmental Sustainability through conservation of these fragile, non-renewable resources.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.4.2.1: Assess importance of Stone Age sites in Zambia (Analysing the importance of Stone Age sites: Tourism, Cultural Heritage).
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners can name and locate Stone Age sites in Zambia (from Lesson 9).

progression.teacherRole: Narrate: "Every year, hundreds of tourists visit Kalambo Falls and nearby caves in Mbala to see evidence of the earliest humans in the region." Ask: "Why do you think people travel from far to see old stones and caves?" State the lesson goal: "Today we explain the importance of Stone Age sites in Zambia."
progression.learnersRole: Give suggestions on why people would travel to see Stone Age sites. Listen attentively to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: Explain tourism importance: Stone Age sites attract local and international tourists and researchers, creating income for local communities (through guiding, crafts, accommodation and food) and for government (through entry fees and taxes), and creating jobs such as tour guides, curators and vendors. Explain cultural heritage importance: these sites preserve evidence of Zambia's earliest history and identity, connecting present-day Zambians to their ancient past and promoting national pride, similar to how Victoria Falls and traditional ceremonies are preserved and celebrated. Explain educational/research importance: sites provide real evidence for historians, archaeologists and learners to study human origins and technological development, supporting education and scientific research both locally and internationally. Explain conservation: because these sites are fragile and non-renewable - once destroyed they cannot be replaced - it is important to protect them from vandalism, indiscriminate mining/quarrying, littering and uncontrolled development, by sensitising communities and involving traditional leaders and heritage clubs. Group Activity: In groups, learners design a simple poster/slogan encouraging Zambians to visit and protect a named Stone Age site, e.g. 'Visit Kalambo Falls - Protect Our Ancient Story', and identify one business opportunity linked to the site. Synthesis: Complete Fig 1.4g on the chalkboard showing Tourism, Cultural Heritage, Education/Research and National recognition.
progression.learnersRole: Take notes on the tourism importance of Stone Age sites. Take notes on the cultural heritage importance of Stone Age sites. Take notes on the educational/research importance of Stone Age sites. Take notes on ways to conserve Stone Age sites. Work in groups to design a poster/slogan and identify a business opportunity. Copy the completed importance diagram from the chalkboard.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State TWO ways Stone Age sites benefit Zambia through tourism. 2. Why are Stone Age sites important as cultural heritage? 3. Mwaba complains that "old caves and stones with no gold are useless and should be dug up for other uses." Using what you have learnt about the importance of Stone Age sites, explain to Mwaba TWO reasons why he is wrong. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Junior Council at your school near Nachikufu Caves in Mpika. The District Tourism Office has invited your council to advise on how to promote and protect the caves for both tourism and future generations. Task 1: Explain TWO ways Nachikufu Caves, or a similar Stone Age site, could generate income for the local community through tourism. (8 marks) Task 2: Explain TWO reasons why such a site is important as part of Zambia's cultural heritage. (6 marks) Task 3: Suggest TWO measures the community/council could take to protect the site from destruction. (6 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Write a half-page proposal titled 'How My Community Can Benefit From and Protect a Nearby Heritage Site', using at least three points learnt in this topic."
progression.learnersRole: Copy the assignment.

progression.teacherRole: Recap: "Stone Age sites in Zambia are important for tourism, cultural heritage and education, and must be protected for future generations." Preview: "Next, we will begin Topic 1.5: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming."
progression.learnersRole: Listen and review key points. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.topic_name: 1.5 THE BEGINNING AND SPREAD OF IRON WORKING AND FARMING
lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.51 Development of Iron Technology and Farming
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Locating on the map areas of early farming in the Middle (Central) Africa.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to locate on a map at least THREE regions of Middle (Central) Africa associated with the spread of early farming, and explain at least TWO reasons why farming spread from these regions into Zambia.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. A wall map or atlas showing the African continent. Printed/drawn copy of Fig 1.4a (Schematic Map of the Spread of Early Farming). Manila paper and coloured pencils/crayons for group map work. Exercise books.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson builds a bridge from the previous topic on the Stone Age to the new topic on Iron Working and Farming. Before learners can appreciate how farming reached Zambia, they must first locate, on a map, the broad regions of Middle Africa from which early farming communities spread. Using a simple schematic map develops learners' analytical thinking and digital/map-reading competences, which will be applied throughout the rest of the topic.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.5.1.1: Analyse impact of Iron technology in farming.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners already know the way of life of Stone Age communities and the location of Stone Age sites in Zambia, such as Mumbwa Caves and Nachikufu Caves, from the previous topic.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Show learners Fig 1.4a (schematic map) and ask: "From our last topic on the Stone Age, how did our ancestors get their food?" 2. Explain that, over time, some communities stopped depending only on hunting and gathering and began growing crops and keeping animals - this is called farming. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we locate on a map the areas of Middle Africa where early farming began and spread from."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Respond that Stone Age people got food by hunting wild animals and gathering wild fruits, roots and honey. 2. Observe Fig 1.4a closely. 3. Listen attentively to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Define Farming: Explain farming (agriculture) as the deliberate growing of crops and keeping of livestock for food, instead of only depending on hunting and gathering. Write the definition on the chalkboard. 2.
