Using Fig 1.4a, explain that historians and archaeologists believe early farming skills began in the region around the Nigeria-Cameroon borderlands of West Africa (the original homeland of the Bantu-speaking peoples), and gradually spread into Central Africa (the Congo Basin), then into Katanga in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and further into East Africa's Great Lakes region, before reaching Zambia. 3. Real-Life Example: Compare this ancient spread with a modern example familiar to learners - just as farming knowledge and improved seed varieties spread today from agricultural research centres such as the Golden Valley Agricultural Research Trust in Chisamba to farming blocks in Mkushi District, ancient farming knowledge spread gradually from one community to its neighbours over many centuries. 4. Group Activity: Put learners in groups of five. Give each group manila paper. Ask them to copy a simple outline showing West Africa, Central Africa (Congo Basin), Katanga and Zambia, and draw arrows showing the direction farming spread, using Fig 1.4a as a guide. 5. Discuss Reasons for the Spread: Guide learners to identify reasons why farming spread southwards into Zambia: growing population pushing people to search for new fertile land; availability of fertile land near rivers such as the Congo, Luapula and Zambezi; exchange of farming knowledge and crops between neighbouring communities through trade and intermarriage; and the desire for a more reliable food supply than hunting and gathering could offer. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the spread of farming and the reasons for its spread on the chalkboard, using the labelled map.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Copy the definition of farming into their notebooks. 2. Trace the route of the spread of farming on Fig 1.4a, from West Africa through Central Africa and Katanga into Zambia. 3. Relate the ancient spread of farming knowledge to the modern spread of farming knowledge from research centres to districts like Mkushi. 4. Work in groups to draw and label the simplified spread map on manila paper. 5. Suggest and note down reasons why farming spread into Zambia, e.g. population growth, fertile land near rivers, exchange of knowledge. 6. Copy the summarised map and reasons into their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. What is the meaning of farming? 2. Name any TWO regions of Middle Africa associated with the early spread of farming. 3. Chomba, a Form 1 pupil at the school, says that people in Zambia have always farmed since the very beginning of human history, and that farming did not come from anywhere else. Using what you have learnt, explain to Chomba TWO reasons why this statement is not entirely correct. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Heritage Club at your school and have been asked to prepare a short talk for Form 1 pupils during Heritage Week on the origins of farming in Zambia. Task 1: Explain the meaning of farming. (2 marks) Task 2: Identify TWO regions in Middle Africa linked to the spread of early farming. (2 marks) Task 3: Explain ONE reason why farming spread from these regions into Zambia. (2 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Using an atlas or a map of Africa, draw a simple sketch map showing Zambia and Middle (Central) Africa. Draw an arrow to show the direction in which early farming spread. Write TWO sentences explaining your drawing."
progression.learnersRole: Copy assignment and complete at home using an atlas.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Farming spread gradually from Middle Africa, through Central Africa and Katanga, into Zambia, driven by population growth and the search for fertile land." 2. Preview: "Next, we will locate on the map the areas of Middle Africa where iron working began and spread from."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.topic_name: 1.5 THE BEGINNING AND SPREAD OF IRON WORKING AND FARMING
lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.51 Development of Iron Technology and Farming
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Locating on the map areas of Iron working in the Middle (Central) Africa.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to locate on a map at least TWO areas of Middle (Central) Africa associated with early iron working, and explain in simple terms the process of iron smelting.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. A wall map or atlas showing the African continent. Printed/drawn copy of Fig 1.4b (Cross-Section of a Traditional Iron Smelting Furnace). A real iron object such as a hoe blade or nail (as a prop). Manila paper for group work.
lesson_plans.rationale: Building on the previous lesson's spread of farming, this lesson introduces iron technology as a skill that spread alongside farming. Understanding the smelting process and the geographic spread of iron working gives learners the technical foundation needed before they study specific Iron Age farming settlements in Zambia in later lessons.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.5.1.1: Analyse impact of Iron technology in farming.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners can locate on a map the regions of Middle Africa associated with the spread of early farming (from the previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Show learners a real iron object, e.g. a hoe blade or a nail. Ask: "What is this tool made of? Where do you think iron comes from?" 2. Link to the previous lesson: "We saw that farming spread from Middle Africa into Zambia. Today we look at how another important skill - iron working - also spread, often together with farming." 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we locate the areas where iron working began, and learn how iron was made."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Observe the iron object and suggest it is made from metal/iron, mined from rocks. 2. Recall that farming spread from Middle Africa into Zambia. 3. Listen attentively to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Define Iron Working: Explain iron working (iron technology) as the process of extracting iron from iron ore found in rocks, and shaping it into tools and weapons through smelting and forging. Write the definition on the chalkboard. 2. Using Fig 1.4b, explain the smelting process step by step: mining iron ore; building a tall clay furnace; stacking alternating layers of charcoal and iron ore inside the furnace; using bellows (often made of goat-skin) connected to clay pipes called tuyeres to pump air and raise the temperature above 1100C; the ore melts and separates into a spongy lump of iron called a bloom, with waste material (slag) draining out at the base; and finally a blacksmith hammers and forges the bloom into tools such as hoes, axes and spears. 3. Explain that iron working, like farming, is believed to have spread from West Africa (the Nok culture area, in present-day Nigeria) through Central Africa, into the iron-and-copper-rich region of Katanga in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and then into Zambia - often carried by the same Bantu-speaking migrating communities who brought farming. 4. Real-Life Example: Compare the ancient blacksmith to blacksmiths (bashikaunga) still found in some Zambian communities today, for example at Mkushi Boma market, who forge hoes, axes and knives using charcoal fires and hammers, showing that the skill of iron working has continued for many centuries. 5. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners draw a simple map showing the spread of iron working from West Africa through Katanga into Zambia, similar to the farming spread map from the previous lesson, and label Katanga as an iron-and-copper-rich area. 6. Synthesis: With class input, label the parts of the furnace diagram (ore, charcoal, tuyeres, bellows, bloom, slag) on the chalkboard.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Copy the definition of iron working/iron technology. 2. Follow the explanation of the smelting process and take notes with the help of Fig 1.4b. 3. Note that iron working spread alongside farming from West Africa through Katanga into Zambia. 4. Relate the ancient blacksmith to modern-day blacksmiths in their community, e.g. at Mkushi Boma market. 5. Work in groups to draw and label the spread map, marking Katanga as an important iron-and-copper-rich region. 6. Help label the parts of the furnace diagram on the chalkboard and copy it into their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. What is iron working (iron technology)? 2. Name any TWO areas of Middle Africa associated with early iron working. 3. Kalaba is confused about why history lessons study iron working and farming together, since one is about metal and the other is about crops. Explain to Kalaba TWO reasons why iron working and farming are studied together as part of the same historical development. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the History Club at the school preparing a display board about how iron was made in the past, for the school's Cultural Day exhibition. Task 1: Describe TWO materials needed to smelt iron in a traditional furnace. (4 marks) Task 2: Briefly explain how iron was extracted using a traditional furnace. (4 marks) Task 3: State ONE importance of iron working to early communities. (2 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Ask an elderly relative or a community member in Mkushi District or your home village whether there were traditional blacksmiths (bashikaunga) in the past. Write THREE sentences about what you found out."
progression.learnersRole: Copy assignment and plan the interview with a family/community elder.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Iron working, like farming, spread from West Africa through Katanga into Zambia, and involved smelting iron ore in a furnace to produce tools." 2. Preview: "Next, we will identify the first Iron Age farming settlement in Zambia: Kalundu."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.topic_name: 1.5 THE BEGINNING AND SPREAD OF IRON WORKING AND FARMING
lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.51 Development of Iron Technology and Farming
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Identifying settlement of Iron Age farmers in Zambia: Kalundu.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to describe the location of Kalundu and state at least THREE features of the Kalundu Iron Age farming settlement.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed/drawn copy of Fig 1.4c (Map of Zambia showing Iron Age farming settlements). Printed/drawn copy of Fig 1.4g (Stone Age tools compared with Iron Age tools). Manila paper divided into two columns. Exercise books.
lesson_plans.rationale: Having learnt how farming and iron working spread into Zambia in general terms, learners now examine specific, concrete evidence of an early Iron Age farming settlement within Zambia itself. Studying Kalundu roots the abstract migration story in tangible Zambian heritage, building citizenship values and pride in the nation's history.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.5.1.1: Analyse impact of Iron technology in farming.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand how farming and iron technology spread into Zambia from Middle Africa (from the previous two lessons).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Show Fig 1.4c and ask: "Which of these towns have you heard of? Where is Kalomo/Choma found in Zambia?" 2. Explain: "Today we study the first and one of the earliest Zambian Iron Age farming settlements - Kalundu." 3. State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Identify Kalomo and Choma on the map as towns in Southern Province. 2. Listen attentively to the introduction. 3. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Location: Using Fig 1.4c, locate Kalundu near the town of Kalomo, in Southern Province, close to Choma. 2. Explain that Kalundu is regarded as one of the earliest Iron Age farming village sites discovered in Zambia, dating from around AD 300, and that it gives its name to the 'Kalundu Tradition', a style of pottery and farming culture found across much of Southern Zambia. 3. Features of Kalundu: guide learners to note that people at Kalundu lived in permanent villages (unlike the mobile camps of Stone Age hunter-gatherers), built pole-and-mud houses, practised mixed farming (growing crops such as sorghum and millet, and keeping cattle, goats and sheep), used iron tools such as hoes and spears, and made distinctive pottery. Archaeologists also found large mounds built up over generations from village rubbish, showing long-term settlement in one place. 4. Compare with the Stone Age: using Fig 1.4g, contrast the permanent, food-producing life at Kalundu with the mobile, foraging life of Stone Age communities such as the Bushmen (San). 5. Group Activity: In groups, learners draw a two-column chart in their exercise books headed 'Stone Age Way of Life' and 'Kalundu Way of Life' and list at least three points under each column. 6. Real-Life Connection: Explain that the modern Kalomo/Choma area is still well known today for cattle-keeping among the Tonga people, showing a continuity of farming and cattle-keeping traditions from the ancient Kalundu farmers to the present day.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Locate Kalomo and Kalundu on Fig 1.4c. 2. Take notes on the dating and significance of Kalundu and the 'Kalundu Tradition'. 3. Note down the features of the Kalundu settlement: permanent villages, pole-and-mud houses, mixed farming, iron tools and pottery. 4. Compare Kalundu's way of life with the Stone Age way of life using Fig 1.4g. 5. Complete the two-column comparison chart in groups. 6. Relate the ancient Kalundu farmers to the modern cattle-keeping Tonga communities around Kalomo and Choma today.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Where is Kalundu found in Zambia? 2. State any TWO features of the Kalundu Iron Age farming settlement. 3. Natasha argues that people at Kalundu lived exactly the same way as Stone Age people because both groups lived in Zambia long ago. Explain to Natasha TWO ways in which life at Kalundu was different from Stone Age life. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a tour guide trainee based in Kalomo, Southern Province. A group of tourists from Lusaka has come to learn about the area's ancient history before visiting the local cattle auction. Task 1: Explain where Kalundu is located. (2 marks) Task 2: Describe TWO features of the way of life of the people who lived at Kalundu. (4 marks) Task 3: Suggest ONE way the modern community around Kalomo could benefit economically from promoting the Kalundu heritage site to tourists. (4 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Using a Social Studies or Geography atlas, find out which present-day province and district Kalomo is found in. Write the province and district in your exercise book."
progression.learnersRole: Copy assignment and complete using an atlas.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Kalundu, near Kalomo, is one of the earliest known Iron Age farming settlements in Zambia, with permanent villages, mixed farming and iron tools." 2. Preview: "Next, we will study another important site in the Kalomo area: Isamu Pati."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.topic_name: 1.5 THE BEGINNING AND SPREAD OF IRON WORKING AND FARMING
lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.51 Development of Iron Technology and Farming
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Identifying settlement of Iron Age farmers in Zambia: Isamu Pati in Kalomo.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to describe the location of Isamu Pati and compare it with Kalundu, stating at least TWO similarities between the two settlements.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed/drawn copy of Fig 1.4c and Fig 1.4d. Manila paper divided into two columns (headed Kalundu / Isamu Pati). Exercise books.
lesson_plans.rationale: Continuing the study of specific Zambian Iron Age sites, Isamu Pati offers a comparative case study within the same Kalomo area. This lesson allows learners to practise the comparison skills already developed in the Stone Age topic, reinforcing analytical thinking and communication competences.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.5.1.1: Analyse impact of Iron technology in farming.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners know the location and features of the Kalundu settlement (from the previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap Kalundu quickly with an oral question-and-answer: "Where is Kalundu, and name one feature of life there." 2. Introduce: "Not far from Kalundu, near the same town of Kalomo, archaeologists found another important settlement called Isamu Pati. Today we learn about it." 3. State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Recall that Kalundu is near Kalomo and that people there practised mixed farming. 2. Listen attentively to the introduction of Isamu Pati. 3. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Location: Locate Isamu Pati on Fig 1.4c as a mound site near Kalomo town, close to Kalundu, in Southern Province. 2. Explain that Isamu Pati is also an Early Iron Age farming village site. Excavations revealed a large mound built up from generations of village waste, dung and collapsed house remains - evidence of a long period of continuous occupation. 3. Features: guide learners to note that, like Kalundu, the people of Isamu Pati practised mixed farming (crops and cattle-keeping), used iron tools, and made pottery in the same 'Kalundu Tradition' style. This shows the early Iron Age society in Southern Zambia was made up of a network of related, neighbouring farming communities rather than a single isolated village. 4. Use Fig 1.4d to show learners the approximate time period during which Kalundu and Isamu Pati flourished (roughly AD 400-900). 5. Group Activity: In pairs, learners fill in a two-column chart comparing Kalundu and Isamu Pati under the headings 'Similarities' and 'Differences', noting that the two sites are very similar since they belong to the same farming tradition and period. 6. Real-Life Example: Compare this cluster of related ancient villages to how modern Mkushi District today has several farming blocks and villages, such as the areas around Mkushi Boma and the surrounding commercial farms, all belonging to the same farming community and district.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Locate Isamu Pati near Kalomo on Fig 1.4c. 2. Note the evidence of long occupation shown by the mound at Isamu Pati. 3. List the features of Isamu Pati: mixed farming, iron tools, pottery in the Kalundu Tradition style. 4. Read the timeline in Fig 1.4d and note the approximate period of Kalundu and Isamu Pati. 5. Complete the two-column comparison chart in pairs. 6. Relate the cluster of Kalomo-area sites to the cluster of farming villages found in modern Mkushi District.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Where is Isamu Pati located? 2. State ONE similarity between Kalundu and Isamu Pati. 3. Bwalya says archaeologists must be mistaken, because 'how can two ancient villages exist so close to each other?' Explain to Bwalya why it is reasonable for Kalundu and Isamu Pati to have existed near each other. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Ministry of Tourism is planning a 'Kalomo Heritage Trail' linking the Kalundu and Isamu Pati mound sites for visitors. As a member of the local Heritage Committee: Task 1: State the location of Isamu Pati. (2 marks) Task 2: Explain TWO features that Isamu Pati and Kalundu have in common. (4 marks) Task 3: Suggest ONE activity that could be included on the Heritage Trail to attract visitors. (4 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Draw a simple sketch showing Kalomo town with two dots labelled Kalundu and Isamu Pati close to each other. Write ONE sentence explaining why archaeologists believe both sites were inhabited by related farming communities."
progression.learnersRole: Copy assignment and complete the sketch and explanation at home.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Isamu Pati, near Kalundu, shares many features with Kalundu and confirms that Southern Zambia had a network of early Iron Age farming villages." 2. Preview: "Next, we move to a different, later and more famous Iron Age settlement: Ing'ombe Ilede."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.topic_name: 1.5 THE BEGINNING AND SPREAD OF IRON WORKING AND FARMING
lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.51 Development of Iron Technology and Farming
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Identifying settlement of Iron Age farmers in Zambia: Ing'ombe Ilede.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to describe the location of Ing'ombe Ilede and state at least THREE features of the settlement, including its famous grave finds.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed/drawn copy of Fig 1.4c and Fig 1.4d. Manila paper for group work. Exercise books.
lesson_plans.rationale: Ing'ombe Ilede represents a later, wealthier and more complex Iron Age settlement, quite different from the simple farming villages of Kalundu and Isamu Pati. Studying its features first prepares learners to understand, in the next lesson, why this site became so wealthy through global trade.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.5.1.1: Analyse impact of Iron technology in farming.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners know the features of the Kalundu and Isamu Pati settlements (from the previous two lessons).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Show the location of Ing'ombe Ilede on Fig 1.4c, near the Zambezi/Lusitu confluence, close to modern-day Siavonga. Ask: "Who has ever visited Siavonga or Lake Kariba? What do you know about that area?" 2. Explain: "Today we learn about Ing'ombe Ilede, a very special and much later Iron Age site found near there." 3. State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Share what they know about Siavonga and Lake Kariba, e.g. fishing, the Kariba Dam. 2. Listen attentively. 3. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Location: Explain precisely that Ing'ombe Ilede is found near the confluence of the Zambezi and Lusitu Rivers, in the Gwembe Valley, Southern Province, near present-day Siavonga. 2. Explain that Ing'ombe Ilede is a Later Iron Age site, much more recent than Kalundu and Isamu Pati, dating from around the 14th to the 17th century AD, and is famous for its extremely rich burials. 3. Describe key features: graves at Ing'ombe Ilede contained gold bangles and ornaments, copper cross-shaped and bar-shaped ingots (used as a form of currency), iron tools and gongs, as well as imported items such as glass beads and cowrie shells - showing that the people buried there were wealthy and held high social status. 4. Explain the significance: unlike the simple farming villages of Kalundu and Isamu Pati, Ing'ombe Ilede shows social stratification (differences between rich and ordinary people) and specialisation of labour (traders, metal workers), indicating a more complex society, likely an important trade and possibly a chiefly/royal burial centre. 5. Group Activity: In groups, learners list at least four items found in the Ing'ombe Ilede graves and sort them into two categories: 'Local Items' (gold, copper, iron) and 'Imported Items' (glass beads, cowrie shells). 6. Real-Life Connection: Compare this to how important traditional leaders in Zambia today, such as chiefs, are honoured with special regalia and ceremonies, showing a continuity of honouring important people in society, though today's ceremonies are conducted with great respect and according to modern customs.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Locate Ing'ombe Ilede near the Zambezi/Lusitu confluence, close to Siavonga, on Fig 1.4c. 2. Note that Ing'ombe Ilede is a Later Iron Age site, dated much later than Kalundu and Isamu Pati. 3. List the items found in the graves: gold ornaments, copper ingots, iron tools/gongs, glass beads, cowrie shells. 4. Discuss what these finds suggest about the wealth and status of the people buried there. 5. Sort the items into 'Local' and 'Imported' categories in groups. 6. Relate the honouring of important people at Ing'ombe Ilede to how traditional leaders are honoured in Zambia today.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Where is Ing'ombe Ilede located? 2. Name any TWO items found in the graves at Ing'ombe Ilede. 3. Chola believes Ing'ombe Ilede was just an ordinary, poor farming village like Kalundu. Using evidence from the graves, explain to Chola TWO reasons why Ing'ombe Ilede was different from Kalundu. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are working with the National Heritage Conservation Commission and have been assigned to write a short exhibition caption for the Ing'ombe Ilede burial finds at the Livingstone Museum. Task 1: State the location of Ing'ombe Ilede. (2 marks) Task 2: Describe TWO items found in the graves and what they suggest about the people buried there. (6 marks) Task 3: Explain ONE reason why it is important to protect and conserve such burial sites for future generations. (2 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Write a paragraph imagining you are an archaeologist who has just opened one of the Ing'ombe Ilede graves. Describe THREE items you find and how you feel about the discovery."
progression.learnersRole: Copy assignment and write the paragraph at home.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Ing'ombe Ilede was a wealthy, later Iron Age settlement near Siavonga, with rich graves containing both local and imported items." 2. Preview: "Next, we will find out how Ing'ombe Ilede was connected to the global trade environment."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.topic_name: 1.5 THE BEGINNING AND SPREAD OF IRON WORKING AND FARMING
lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.51 Development of Iron Technology and Farming
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Relating Ing'ombe Ilede to the global trade environment.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to explain how Ing'ombe Ilede was linked to global (Indian Ocean) trade, naming at least TWO goods exported and TWO goods imported.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed/drawn copy of Fig 1.4e (Ing'ombe Ilede and the Global Trade Network). A wall map or atlas showing Africa and the Indian Ocean. Manila paper for group work.
lesson_plans.rationale: Building on the previous lesson's description of Ing'ombe Ilede's wealth, this lesson explains why the settlement was so wealthy - its links to regional and international trade networks. This helps learners appreciate Zambia's place in world history and understand that long-distance global connections existed centuries before colonial rule.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.5.1.1: Analyse impact of Iron technology in farming.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners know the features and grave finds of Ing'ombe Ilede (from the previous lesson).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Ask: "The imported items we discussed last lesson - glass beads and cowrie shells - did not come from Zambia. Where do you think they came from?" 2. Explain: "Today's lesson explains the trade routes and network that connected Ing'ombe Ilede to the wider world." 3. State the lesson goal.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Suggest that the beads and shells may have come from another country or across the sea. 2. Listen attentively. 3. Listen to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Using Fig 1.4e, explain the trade network: traders at Ing'ombe Ilede exchanged local goods, such as gold, copper, ivory, salt and iron goods, with Swahili Coast traders on the East African coast (present-day Tanzania/Mozambique area). 2. Explain that Swahili Coast traders then linked with Indian Ocean dhow trade routes, connecting Ing'ombe Ilede's goods, indirectly, as far as India and Arabia. 3. Explain what came IN to Ing'ombe Ilede through this network: glass beads, cowrie shells and cloth, which were highly valued and used for decoration and possibly as a form of wealth or currency. 4. Explain the likely trade process: goods probably moved along the Zambezi River and overland caravan routes to coastal towns such as Sofala, before being carried by dhow across the Indian Ocean. 5. Group Activity: In groups, learners use Fig 1.4e to draw two lists - 'Goods OUT of Ing'ombe Ilede' and 'Goods IN to Ing'ombe Ilede' - then discuss the question: "What does this trade tell us about how developed pre-colonial Zambian society was?" 6. Real-Life Connection: Compare this ancient trade to modern Zambian international trade, for example copper exports today from the Copperbelt Province to international markets, showing that Zambia's mineral wealth has been valued internationally for many centuries.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Take notes on the goods traded OUT of Ing'ombe Ilede to Swahili Coast traders. 2. Note that Swahili traders linked Ing'ombe Ilede to the wider Indian Ocean trade network. 3. List the goods traded IN to Ing'ombe Ilede: glass beads, cowrie shells, cloth. 4. Trace the likely trade route on the wall map, from the Zambezi River to the coast. 5. Work in groups to list export and import goods and discuss the level of development of pre-colonial Zambian society. 6. Relate the ancient gold/copper trade to modern copper exports from the Copperbelt.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name ONE item that was exported OUT of Ing'ombe Ilede. 2. Name ONE item that was imported INTO Ing'ombe Ilede from the Indian Ocean trade. 3. Mwansa believes pre-colonial Zambians never had any contact with the outside world before Europeans arrived. Using evidence from Ing'ombe Ilede, correct Mwansa's view. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: As a Form 1 History Ambassador at the school, you have been asked to explain to visiting exchange learners from a school in Ndola how Zambia was connected to the rest of the world long before colonial times. Task 1: Name TWO goods that Ing'ombe Ilede exported to the East African coast. (4 marks) Task 2: Name TWO goods that Ing'ombe Ilede imported from overseas via the Indian Ocean trade. (4 marks) Task 3: Explain what this trade tells us about pre-colonial Zambian society. (2 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Using an atlas, trace on a simple sketch map the route goods might have travelled from Ing'ombe Ilede (near Siavonga) to the Indian Ocean coast. Label the Zambezi River and the coast."
progression.learnersRole: Copy assignment and complete the sketch map at home using an atlas.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Ing'ombe Ilede was connected, through Swahili Coast traders, to the wider Indian Ocean trade network reaching as far as India and Arabia." 2. Preview: "Next, we will analyse the importance of iron technology, starting with agriculture and trade."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.topic_name: 1.5 THE BEGINNING AND SPREAD OF IRON WORKING AND FARMING
lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.51 Development of Iron Technology and Farming
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Analysing the importance of Iron technology in Agriculture and Trade.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to explain at least TWO ways iron technology improved agriculture and TWO ways it boosted trade in early Zambian society.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed/drawn copy of Fig 1.4f and Fig 1.4g. A real hoe or axe, if available, for demonstration. Manila paper divided into two columns.
lesson_plans.rationale: Having studied specific settlements and trade networks, learners now analyse WHY iron technology mattered so much, connecting iron tools directly to increased food production and to trade, which reinforces financial literacy and entrepreneurship competences alongside historical understanding.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.5.1.1: Analyse impact of Iron technology in farming.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the iron smelting process (from Lesson 2) and the trade connections of Ing'ombe Ilede (from Lesson 6).

progression.teacherRole: 1. Show Fig 1.4g (Stone Age tools versus Iron Age tools). Ask: "Which tools would clear a farm faster - stone tools or iron tools? Why?" 2. State the lesson goal: "Today we analyse how iron tools improved farming and boosted trade in early Zambian society."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Respond that iron tools would clear land faster because they are sharper and stronger than stone tools. 2. Listen attentively to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Agriculture: explain that iron hoes and axes allowed farmers to clear larger areas of bush and forest faster than stone tools, and to till the soil more effectively. This led to larger farms, more food produced, food surpluses, population growth and permanent settlements, as seen at Kalundu and Isamu Pati. 2. Trade: explain that iron tools themselves became trade items, as skilled blacksmiths made surplus hoes, axes and spears to exchange with neighbouring communities for goods such as salt, cattle and pottery. Iron goods, together with copper and gold, also became part of the long-distance trade goods exported from settlements such as Ing'ombe Ilede. 3. Real-Life Example: Compare this to modern Zambia, where Mkushi and Kalomo Districts remain major agricultural producing areas today, now using tractors and other modern machinery instead of iron hoes - showing continuity in the idea that better tools lead to greater farming output. 4. Case Example: Describe a hypothetical, realistic example - a blacksmith family living near pre-colonial Kalomo producing surplus iron hoes and trading them with neighbouring Tonga cattle-keepers in exchange for cattle, directly linking iron production to trade. 5. Group Activity: In groups, learners list on manila paper THREE ways iron tools improved farming and TWO ways iron goods boosted trade, then present their findings to the class. 6. Synthesis: With class input, complete the Agriculture and Trade segments of the Fig 1.4f wheel diagram on the chalkboard.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Take notes on how iron hoes and axes improved farming, leading to larger farms and food surpluses. 2. Take notes on how iron tools and goods became items of trade. 3. Relate ancient iron-tool farming to modern mechanised farming in Mkushi and Kalomo Districts. 4. Follow the case example of a blacksmith family trading hoes for cattle. 5. Work in groups to list and present ways iron technology improved farming and trade. 6. Help complete the Agriculture and Trade segments of the wheel diagram and copy it into their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE way iron technology improved agriculture. 2. State ONE way iron technology boosted trade. 3. Chulu says using an iron hoe is not very different from using a wooden digging stick. Explain to Chulu TWO reasons why this statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are an Entrepreneurship Club member at the school organising a 'Then and Now' exhibition comparing pre-colonial and modern farming tools. Task 1: Explain how the iron hoe improved farming compared to Stone Age tools. (4 marks) Task 2: Explain how iron tools became items of trade in early Zambian society. (4 marks) Task 3: Suggest ONE modern farming tool that has replaced the iron hoe today, and state ONE advantage of the modern tool. (2 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Interview a farmer in your community, in Mkushi District or your home area, about which farming tools they use today. Write TWO sentences comparing their tools to the iron hoe used by early Iron Age farmers."
progression.learnersRole: Copy assignment and conduct the interview at home.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Iron technology improved agriculture by making land-clearing and tilling faster, and boosted trade through the exchange of surplus iron tools and goods." 2. Preview: "Next, we will complete our analysis of the importance of iron technology, by looking at hunting and fishing, and review the whole topic."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.

lesson_plans.topic_name: 1.5 THE BEGINNING AND SPREAD OF IRON WORKING AND FARMING
lesson_plans.subtopic_name: 1.51 Development of Iron Technology and Farming
lesson_plans.majorLearningPoint: Analysing the importance of Iron technology in Hunting and Fishing, and reviewing Topic 1.5.
lesson_plans.lessonGoal: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to explain at least TWO ways iron technology improved hunting and TWO ways it improved fishing, and summarise the overall importance of iron technology to Iron Age Zambian society.
lesson_plans.references: 2024 History Syllabus, Secondary Education Ordinary Level, Form 1-4 (Topic 1.4: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming).
lesson_plans.tlm: Chalkboard and chalk. Printed/drawn copy of Fig 1.4f (completed wheel). Manila paper for group summary posters. Exercise books.
lesson_plans.rationale: This lesson completes the four-part analysis of the importance of iron technology begun in the previous lesson (agriculture and trade), by examining hunting and fishing. It then consolidates the whole of Topic 1.4 into a final review, helping learners see the full picture of how iron technology and farming transformed early Zambian society.
objectives: Specific Competence 1.5.1.1: Analyse impact of Iron technology in farming.
lesson_plans.priorKnowledge: Learners understand the importance of iron technology in agriculture and trade (from the previous lesson) and have covered all the content of Topic 1.4 from Lessons 1 to 7.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Ask: "Communities living near the Zambezi and Kafue Rivers depended a lot on hunting and fishing. How do you think iron tools changed hunting and fishing compared to Stone Age tools?" 2. State the lesson goal: "Today we complete our study of the importance of iron technology by looking at hunting and fishing, then review the whole topic."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Suggest that iron tools made hunting and fishing easier and more effective than stone or wooden tools. 2. Listen attentively to the lesson goal.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Hunting: explain that iron spear heads and arrow heads were sharper, stronger and more effective than stone-tipped weapons, making hunting safer and more successful, and providing more meat and hides for early Iron Age communities. Refer to Fig 1.4g from Lesson 7 to recall the tool comparison. 2. Fishing: explain that iron fish hooks and harpoons allowed communities living along rivers such as the Zambezi, Kafue and Luangwa to catch more fish more effectively than earlier wooden traps and bone spears, supporting riverine communities like those who later thrived at Ing'ombe Ilede near the Zambezi/Lusitu confluence. 3. Complete Fig 1.4f: with class discussion, complete all four segments of the wheel diagram (Agriculture, Trade, Hunting, Fishing) on the chalkboard, showing how iron technology transformed almost every part of Iron Age life. 4. Whole-Topic Review Activity: In groups, learners create a summary poster on manila paper covering the whole of Topic 1.4: the spread of farming and iron working into Zambia (Lessons 1-2), Kalundu, Isamu Pati and Ing'ombe Ilede (Lessons 3-5), the global trade of Ing'ombe Ilede (Lesson 6), and the importance of iron technology (Lessons 7-8). 5. Gallery Walk: groups display their posters around the classroom; learners walk round in an orderly manner to read other groups' summaries. 6. Real-Life Example: mention that modern fishing communities along the Zambezi, for example at Siavonga near Lake Kariba, still use hooks and nets today, though the materials have advanced to include nylon nets, showing continuity from Iron Age fishing methods to the present.
progression.learnersRole: 1. Take notes on how iron spear and arrow heads improved hunting. 2. Take notes on how iron fish hooks and harpoons improved fishing along major rivers. 3. Help complete the four-segment wheel diagram (agriculture, trade, hunting, fishing) and copy it into their notebooks. 4. Work in groups to create a summary poster covering the whole of Topic 1.4. 5. Participate in the gallery walk, reading and discussing other groups' posters. 6. Relate ancient river fishing to modern fishing along the Zambezi/Lake Kariba today.

progression.teacherRole: Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE way iron technology improved hunting. 2. State ONE way iron technology improved fishing. 3. Mutinta says fishing and hunting are not really 'history' topics because people still do them today. Explain to Mutinta why studying the history of hunting and fishing tools is still important. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your school's History Club has been asked to present a wall chart titled 'How Iron Technology Changed Zambia' at the Provincial Education Day in Kabwe. Task 1: Explain how iron technology improved hunting among Early Iron Age communities. (4 marks) Task 2: Explain how iron technology improved fishing among communities living along rivers such as the Zambezi. (4 marks) Task 3: Using what you have learnt in this topic, summarise in one paragraph why the spread of iron working and farming was a turning point in Zambia's history. (2 marks)
progression.learnersRole: Read questions. Answer individually in their notebooks.

progression.teacherRole: Assign: "Write a half-page summary titled 'Why Iron Technology Changed Life in Early Zambia', mentioning at least FOUR points from agriculture, trade, hunting and fishing covered in this topic."
progression.learnersRole: Copy assignment and write the summary at home.

progression.teacherRole: 1. Recap: "Iron technology transformed early Zambian society by improving agriculture, boosting trade, and making hunting and fishing more effective and productive." 2. Preview: "Next, we will begin a new topic: 1.5 The Bantu-Speaking People."
progression.learnersRole: 1. Listen and review key points. 2. Anticipate the next topic.
